walkthroughs.body_html:
Practical Techniques — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Practical Techniques brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Practical Techniques.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A car travels 4 km north then 3 km east. What is its displacement magnitude?
options: 7 km
5 km
1 km
25 km

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
options: Acceleration
Momentum
Kinetic energy
Weight

mcqs.q: What property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
options: It showed that alpha particles can pass through any material because they are massless.
The frequency — higher frequency means higher pitch.
The speed of the wave determines pitch — faster waves sound higher.
Amplitude determines pitch — a bigger wave is a higher-pitched note.

mcqs.q: If a car doubles its speed, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: It quadruples (because KE = 1/2 mv^2 — kinetic energy is proportional to v^2).
The speed of the wave determines pitch — faster waves sound higher.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
Kinetic energy doubles because energy is proportional to speed.

mcqs.q: What did Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment show about the atom?
options: Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
It showed that alpha particles can pass through any material because they are massless.
Most of the atom is empty space, with a tiny dense positive nucleus.
It showed that atoms are solid spheres of positive charge with electrons embedded inside.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resolving vectors”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Acceleration”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Velocity”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Displacement”?
options: The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vector”?
options: Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.

free_texts.hint: It's one of the six key terms above.
